title: Beeswarm plots: show individual values without inventing spread
summary: Keep the measured axis exact, treat sideways displacement as layout, and disclose how many marks are present.
body:
Keep the measured axis exact, treat sideways displacement as layout, and disclose how many marks are present.

A dot is an observation

A beeswarm places individual observations along a measured axis and moves marks sideways only enough to reduce overlap. The lateral coordinate is not a second measured variable. State that in the axis caption, because a wide swarm can otherwise be mistaken for more variation. If the mark count exceeds the display's collision capacity, use a declared sample or a distribution summary instead of silently dropping points. Overplotting and sampling bias determine whether the displayed dots still represent the underlying population. Report the raw count and the displayed count for every group.

Preserve ties and identity

Repeated equal measurements should remain repeated observations. A deterministic layout lets an analyst compare revisions without random movement that looks like new data. Stable IDs matter when a reader selects or exports a point. If several rows share the same subject and timestamp, decide whether they are repeated measurements or duplicates before drawing. The plot cannot make that data decision. The export manifest should preserve observation ID, group, measured value, sampling rule and layout version. A text alternative can list the median, range, count and number of tied values.

Collision radius is a visual parameter

A beeswarm solver needs marker diameter in display pixels as well as the scale that maps values to pixels. Zooming, resizing or switching to mobile changes collision geometry. Thus an offset computed for one viewport cannot safely be reused for another. Cap the lateral spread only if the chart explicitly allows overlap after that cap; hiding dots is not acceptable. Accessible mark encodings need a visible outline or shape difference when groups share a panel. Test the chart at the narrowest intended width.

Compare with a distribution summary

The swarm is good for a few hundred visible records, particularly when outliers and ties are the story. At larger scale it becomes slow to lay out and hard to read. A box, violin or ECDF can summarize shape, while a small sample of dots reveals examples without pretending to be complete. Box and violin plots have their own bandwidth and whisker decisions; they are not interchangeable with raw observations. If groups have unequal sample sizes, annotate counts next to labels so width is not mistaken for prevalence.

Worked contract

from hashlib import sha256
from math import isfinite

def stable_strip_positions(records: list[tuple[str, str, float]],
                           spread: float = 0.38) -> list[tuple[str, str, float, float]]:
    if not 0 <= spread <= 0.5:
        raise ValueError("spread must fit inside one category")
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("observation IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not group or not isfinite(value) for _, group, value in records):
        raise ValueError("group and measured value must be valid")
    placed = []
    for record_id, group, value in records:
        digest = sha256(record_id.encode("utf-8")).digest()
        fraction = int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") / (2**64 - 1)
        placed.append((record_id, group, value, (2 * fraction - 1) * spread))
    return placed

service_times = [("ticket-47", "priority", 81.0),
                 ("ticket-59", "priority", 81.0),
                 ("ticket-83", "standard", 97.0)]
positions = stable_strip_positions(service_times)
assert len(positions) == 3 and positions[0][2] == positions[1][2]
assert positions == stable_strip_positions(service_times)

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N stable strip positions takes O(N) expected time and O(N) output space. This code produces reproducible jitter; it is not a collision-solving beeswarm. A true beeswarm needs screen-space marker geometry and may require O(N squared) comparisons in a simple placement algorithm. Do not label the jittered result collision-free. Preserve exact measured values and IDs in the export, and recalculate visual offsets when the display scale changes.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading sideways jitter as a measured quantity.
  • Suppressing overlapped observations without recording the omitted count.
  • Reseeding random positions on every redraw, making stable records appear to move.
  • Calling deterministic jitter a collision-free beeswarm without checking marker radius.

Validation drill

Draw 81 support-ticket response times across three queues. Keep equal values as separate dots, show each queue's count and compare a narrow mobile layout with a distribution summary.

title: Calendar heatmaps: distinguish an empty day from an absent day
summary: Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.
body:
Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.

A blank square has several meanings

A calendar heatmap arranges daily values in a weekly grid. A white day could mean zero events, no feed, a day outside the reporting range or a suppressed value. Those states cannot share one silent color. Generate every expected local date first, then join observations and label each cell's status. Missing-cell heatmaps need the same distinction. For a support operation, a zero confirmed ticket count is evidence; an uncollected Saturday is not. Show the number of complete days beside any annual total.

Choose the reporting day

An event at 00:20 UTC may belong to the prior local day. Convert timestamps to the declared reporting zone before aggregating, and record the zone in the export. Daylight-saving changes produce 23- or 25-hour local days in some regions; counts remain counts, but per-hour rates need an exposure adjustment. A calendar grid without its time-zone contract can move incidents across cells and distort weekday patterns. Time-series calendar rules cover incomplete current periods and delayed arrivals. Mark provisional days rather than painting them as final.

Keep color comparable

Fix the numeric color domain across years or related teams when the goal is comparison. Otherwise each year may assign the darkest shade to a different count. If the distribution has a long tail, state any transform or clipped maximum. A daily rate requires the matching daily denominator; weekend exposure often differs from weekday exposure. Grain and denominator come before color selection. A tooltip should expose date, value, status, denominator if used and refresh time, while a text table remains available for keyboard and screen-reader users.

Week structure is a locale decision

Some audiences expect Monday-first weeks; others expect Sunday-first. Label weekdays, show month boundaries and test leap years, year transitions and ISO week edges. Do not infer a causal weekday pattern from a few colored streaks. A release schedule, holiday closure or data-delivery gap may explain the pattern. Event annotations should state what happened without claiming effect. Export an explicit date-status table so another analyst can reconstruct the image rather than reverse-engineering its colors.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(start: date, end: date,
                          observed: dict[date, int | None]
                          ) -> list[tuple[date, str, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("dates must fall inside the requested period")
    if any(value is not None and (not isinstance(value, int) or value < 0)
           for value in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("daily counts must be nonnegative integers")
    result = []
    day = start
    while day <= end:
        value = observed.get(day)
        status = "missing" if value is None else "observed"
        result.append((day, status, value))
        day += timedelta(days=1)
    return result

calendar_rows = complete_daily_series(
    date(2026, 10, 1), date(2026, 10, 4),
    {date(2026, 10, 1): 47, date(2026, 10, 2): 0,
     date(2026, 10, 4): 59})
assert calendar_rows[1] == (date(2026, 10, 2), "observed", 0)
assert calendar_rows[2] == (date(2026, 10, 3), "missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For D days and O observed keys, validation and completion take O(D+O) time and O(D) output space. This code assumes the input keys already represent the correct reporting-zone dates; timestamp conversion belongs upstream. If a source uses null to mean suppression rather than missing delivery, give it its own status before calling this function. Store daily exposure separately when coloring rates.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning missing days into zeros.
  • Aggregating UTC dates and labeling the result as a local calendar.
  • Allowing each year to auto-scale its colors during comparison.
  • Treating a partly reported current day as final.

Validation drill

Build a 47-day operations calendar with a confirmed zero, a late feed, a holiday closure and one provisional day. Export the four states and explain the color domain.

title: Parallel coordinates: make every axis conversion inspectable
summary: Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.
body:
Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.

A polyline is one record

Parallel coordinates display one entity as a line crossing several vertical axes. Its crossings are the entity's values; line slopes between axes are visual connectors, not measured rates of change. Before drawing, name every metric and unit. A route whose five service measures have incompatible units cannot be read honestly on one raw height scale. Scale integrity applies independently to every axis. Put the raw value in a tooltip or adjacent table so a normalized line does not erase the original measurement.

Normalization changes the question

Min-max normalization maps each axis to a shared display interval, but a single extreme entity can compress all others. Fixed policy bounds may be more stable than bounds computed from the current filter. If lower is preferable for one metric, invert its display direction and label that inversion. Never silently reverse an axis just to make good records form a tidy line. Target-oriented KPI charts may be clearer if the decision is only whether a threshold was met. Keep the bounds, direction and unit beside each dimension in exported metadata.

Axis order and brushing are analytic choices

Swapping two adjacent axes changes which relationships are visually easiest to see, even though the data stay unchanged. Pick an order tied to the question, such as intake, response, resolution and cost, then preserve it across comparable views. Brushing one range selects entities; a linked table should show which IDs remain and how many were excluded. Linked filters require explicit cohort state. Avoid drawing every record at full opacity: a thousand crossing lines become an opaque band. Sampling must retain a visible selected count and a full-population summary.

Missing values must not become fabricated paths

A line should break or be omitted with an explicit reason when one dimension is absent; zero is not a replacement for missing. Check whether the missingness is related to the outcome being inspected. If only high-cost projects fail to report quality, excluding incomplete records changes the apparent relationship. An export manifest should name complete-case rules, filter state, axis order, bounds and transformed values. For accessibility, offer a sortable table of the underlying records and a concise summary of which dimensions separate selected groups.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def normalize_profile(profile: dict[str, float | None],
                      axes: dict[str, tuple[float, float, bool]]
                      ) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    if set(profile) != set(axes):
        raise ValueError("profile dimensions must match axis declarations")
    normalized = {}
    for metric, (low, high, lower_is_better) in axes.items():
        value = profile[metric]
        if not all(isfinite(bound) for bound in (low, high)) or high <= low:
            raise ValueError("axis bounds must be finite and ordered")
        if value is None:
            normalized[metric] = None
            continue
        if not isfinite(value) or not low <= value <= high:
            raise ValueError("measurement outside declared axis")
        position = (value - low) / (high - low)
        normalized[metric] = 1 - position if lower_is_better else position
    return normalized

axes = {"response_minutes": (0, 120, True),
        "resolved_percent": (0, 100, False)}
depot_profile = normalize_profile(
    {"response_minutes": 47, "resolved_percent": 81}, axes)
assert round(depot_profile["response_minutes"], 4) == 0.6083
assert depot_profile["resolved_percent"] == 0.81

Performance and operating cost

For D dimensions in one record, normalization takes O(D) time and O(D) output space; N records take O(ND). Rendering N polylines can dominate interaction cost, especially when brushing triggers full redraws. The code rejects values outside policy bounds rather than clipping them invisibly. If clipping is intended, export both raw and displayed values and count clipped records by axis.

Common Mistakes

  • Interpreting connector slope as a real-world rate of change.
  • Recomputing axis bounds after a filter and comparing line heights as if scale stayed fixed.
  • Silently reversing one axis or replacing missing with zero.
  • Drawing all records at full opacity and calling the dense band a cluster.

Validation drill

Compare 59 depots on response time, resolution rate and cost. Publish fixed axis bounds, invert only metrics where lower is better, then brush a subgroup and reconcile its ID count to the table.

  • Bullet charts: show a measure, target and performance bands honestly

title: Bump charts: show rank movement without losing ties or entrants
summary: Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.
body:
Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.

Rank is an ordering, not a magnitude

A bump chart connects an entity's ranks across periods. A move from third to first may reflect a tiny absolute difference or a major change; the line does not tell you which. Name the ranked measure and link to values behind each position. Paired-change charts work better when the actual size of change matters. If a new entity enters the cohort, existing ranks can fall without their own measurements changing. Display entrants and exits as membership events rather than implying deterioration.

Ties need a written rule

Equal measurements can share a rank, be assigned adjacent ranks by a secondary key, or be shown in a tied band. These choices produce different line paths. Competition ranking gives equal values the same rank and skips the next position; dense ranking does not skip. Neither should be selected by accident inside a plotting library. Preserve raw values and the chosen tie rule in the export. Reproducible chart exports also need source period and eligibility criteria. Test ties at both top and bottom before publishing.

Hold the cohort question steady

A panel can rank the same fixed set of entities every period or rank whoever was eligible at the time. The first view tracks a stable cohort; the second reflects changing membership. State which one readers see. If a missing measurement removes an entity from one period, show a line break or missing marker rather than assigning last place. Provisional periods and data gaps are especially easy to hide in a rank-only display. Mark a period as provisional when its numerator or denominator can still change.

Limit crossings and preserve access

Many crossing lines defeat tracing. Highlight a small set chosen by a documented rule, fade the remainder and let the reader search by entity ID. A table with period, rank, value and membership status is essential, because color-only line identity and hover-only labels fail on touch and assistive technology. Text alternatives should call out the biggest rank rise, biggest fall, ties and entrants. Do not claim a trend from two ranks alone; a third period or actual values may tell a different story.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def competition_ranks(scores: dict[str, float]) -> dict[str, int]:
    if any(not entity for entity in scores):
        raise ValueError("entity IDs must be nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in scores.values()):
        raise ValueError("scores must be finite")
    ordered = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    ranks = {}
    prior_score = None
    current_rank = 0
    for position, (entity, score) in enumerate(ordered, start=1):
        if prior_score is None or score != prior_score:
            current_rank = position
        ranks[entity] = current_rank
        prior_score = score
    return ranks

week_47 = competition_ranks({"north": 81, "south": 81,
                             "west": 59, "east": 47})
assert week_47 == {"north": 1, "south": 1, "west": 3, "east": 4}

Performance and operating cost

Ranking N entities costs O(N log N) time and O(N) output space per period; connecting P periods takes O(PN) output storage for a fixed cohort. The code uses higher-score-first competition ranks and stable ID ordering only for reproducible output. It does not fill absent entities. Before rendering, validate that every period uses the same score definition and disclose whether the eligible set is fixed or variable.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a one-place rise as a fixed-size improvement.
  • Allowing a chart library to break ties arbitrarily.
  • Assigning missing entities last place.
  • Comparing periods with changing eligibility without labeling entrants and exits.

Validation drill

Rank 47 service depots over six weeks with two ties and one new entrant. Reconcile every rank to its score and show how the entrant changes the apparent position of unchanged depots.

title: P charts: account for varying denominators before flagging a rate
summary: Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.
body:
Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.

A rate needs its opportunity count

A p chart follows a proportion such as defective shipments divided by inspected shipments. Forty-seven defects in 470 inspections and 47 in 4,700 do not carry the same sampling uncertainty. Plot the period denominator or put it in a table, and calculate limits from the baseline proportion using each period's sample size. Denominator discipline is the first check. Do not mix units such as orders and line items, or change the defect definition midway through the series.

Freeze the baseline before judging a new point

Choose a stable historical interval and document excluded outages, policy changes and incomplete periods. Pool baseline defects over baseline opportunities for a center line. Calculating a fresh center from every newly flagged point can move the goalposts. A period beyond an approximate three-standard-error limit is a signal to investigate; it does not prove a specific cause. Event annotations should distinguish observed timing from causal evidence. A confirmed process change may justify a new baseline, but record where the old phase ends.

Know the approximation's limits

The simple p-chart formula assumes independent, comparable Bernoulli opportunities and a fairly stable underlying probability. Correlated batches, rare events or extra variation can make the limits misleading. Tiny sample sizes produce wide limits; values must still stay between zero and one. If repeated points reveal more variation than the model allows, investigate the collection process or choose a method suited to overdispersion. Small-sample displays help communicate why a large-looking percentage swing may be weak evidence. A control limit is not a target or a confidence interval for a business decision.

Explain the chart without color

Show the center line, period-specific bounds, actual rate, numerator and denominator in the export. Mark flagged points with shape and text, not red alone. If a late-arriving batch changes a historical numerator, recompute the affected point and disclose the revision. Provisional periods should be clearly separate from finalized ones. An accessible summary can state which periods crossed limits and which lacked enough data, while leaving the causal diagnosis to the investigation.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def p_chart_rows(baseline: list[tuple[int, int]],
                 periods: list[tuple[str, int, int]]
                 ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float, bool]]:
    def valid(defects: int, inspected: int) -> bool:
        return (isinstance(defects, int) and isinstance(inspected, int)
                and inspected > 0 and 0 <= defects <= inspected)
    if not baseline or any(not valid(d, n) for d, n in baseline):
        raise ValueError("baseline requires valid defect counts")
    if any(not label or not valid(d, n) for label, d, n in periods):
        raise ValueError("period counts or labels are invalid")
    center = sum(d for d, _ in baseline) / sum(n for _, n in baseline)
    output = []
    for label, defects, inspected in periods:
        radius = 3 * sqrt(center * (1 - center) / inspected)
        lower, upper = max(0.0, center - radius), min(1.0, center + radius)
        rate = defects / inspected
        output.append((label, rate, lower, upper, rate < lower or rate > upper))
    return output

baseline = [(47, 470), (59, 590), (81, 810)]
signals = p_chart_rows(baseline, [("week-47", 47, 470),
                                  ("week-48", 3, 470)])
assert round(signals[0][1], 4) == 0.1
assert signals[1][-1] is True

Performance and operating cost

For B baseline periods and P plotted periods, this calculation takes O(B+P) time and O(P) output space. The three-standard-error limits are an approximation under an independent binomial model; the code does not test independence, estimate overdispersion or infer a cause. A production pipeline should version the baseline and defect definition, enforce finalized counts, and show denominator size with every point.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing percentages while concealing sharply different sample sizes.
  • Recomputing the baseline after every flagged period.
  • Calling a control limit a business target.
  • Treating a signal as proof of the annotated event's effect.

Validation drill

Track 59 weekly inspection proportions with variable sample sizes. Freeze a baseline, flag points beyond their own limits and investigate a week whose rate is high but denominator is small.

  • Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
  • Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
  • Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality

Where to begin

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
summary: Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.
body:
Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.

Begin with observations

A box summarizes a group's quartiles and median; a violin adds an estimated density shape. Neither replaces the sample size. A smooth violin made from seven delivery times can look as confident as one made from seven thousand. Put each group's count beside its label and show individual points for small groups. Distribution and outlier displays explain what the summary hides. First check whether groups cover the same window, unit and eligibility rule. Otherwise the apparent difference may be a cohort change.

Declare the quartile rule

Software packages can interpolate quartiles differently, and whiskers may mean the extrema or a multiple of the interquartile range. State the rule in the chart caption or export record. A point beyond a whisker is not automatically bad data; it is flagged under that rule. If the decision needs the fraction exceeding a service threshold, calculate that fraction directly rather than asking a box to imply it. An empirical CDF answers threshold questions without a smoothing choice.

Treat bandwidth as a parameter

A violin's width depends on a density estimate and its bandwidth. A wide bandwidth can merge two real modes; a narrow one can turn routine noise into several peaks. Compare more than one defensible bandwidth, retain a rug or points, and do not imply that a thin tail continues beyond a physical limit. The mirrored shape is a drawing convention, not a second population. Normalize violin widths by count only if width should carry count. Otherwise make widths equal and show counts separately. Grain and denominator still matter.

Keep groups comparable

Use the same quantitative axis, bandwidth rule and density normalization across groups. Truncating each group to its own range can make spreads seem alike. For latency data, inspect zeros, censored values and caps before estimating density. If the data include repeated readings from the same device, an independent violin discards pairing. A paired view retains it. Supply a text table with each count, median, quartiles and threshold exceedance for readers who cannot use the shape.

Worked contract

def quartile_summary(readings: list[float]) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    from math import isfinite
    if not readings or any(not isfinite(value) for value in readings):
        raise ValueError("readings must be finite and nonempty")
    ordered = sorted(readings)
    def midpoint(values: list[float]) -> float:
        middle = len(values) // 2
        return (values[middle] if len(values) % 2 else
                (values[middle - 1] + values[middle]) / 2)
    middle = len(ordered) // 2
    lower = ordered[:middle]
    upper = ordered[middle + len(ordered) % 2:]
    return {"count": len(ordered), "median": midpoint(ordered),
            "q1": midpoint(lower) if lower else ordered[0],
            "q3": midpoint(upper) if upper else ordered[0]}

depot_latency = quartile_summary([47, 51, 59, 68, 81, 83, 96])
assert depot_latency == {"count": 7, "median": 68, "q1": 51, "q3": 83}

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N observations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for the ordered copy. A chart with G groups repeats this per group; density estimation adds work set by the estimator and evaluation grid. The code declares a median-of-halves quartile convention and handles a one-item group. It does not draw a violin or claim that seven points support a smooth density. Store the exact convention with the exported summary.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a smooth violin for a tiny group without points.
  • Comparing boxes whose whiskers use different rules.
  • Treating a flagged point as an invalid measurement.
  • Changing density bandwidth between groups and reading widths as a real difference.

Validation drill

Compare response times for three depots with 7, 47 and 810 records. Print each count, median and quartile rule; draw points for the smallest group, then inspect whether two bandwidth choices alter the visual claim.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
summary: Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.
body:
Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.

Use a meaningful baseline

Bar length is read against its baseline. Starting a bar axis at 0.71 can make two completion rates of 0.74 and 0.77 look several times apart. Use zero for ordinary bar lengths and show exact values when a small difference matters. A line chart may use a narrower range to show variation, but the displayed bounds and units must remain obvious.

Inspect transformations

A logarithmic axis can reveal values across orders of magnitude, but equal screen distances then represent equal ratios rather than equal differences. Zero and negative values need an explicit treatment. Never switch an axis to logarithmic merely to fit an outlier, and never compare a linear-panel slope with a log-panel slope as though they share meaning.

Keep category order honest

Sort categories by a documented metric or a stable domain order. If the order changes at each refresh, motion can look like a performance shift when values are steady. Labels should state percent versus percentage points; moving from 74 to 77 percent is a three-point change, not a three-percent relative change. The chart question decides which comparison is primary.

Test presentation rules

Prepare two rates, 0.74 and 0.77, and verify both bars share zero. Then format them as 74.0% and 77.0%. If a narrow view clips labels, retain an accessible text table. Recheck after filtering because an automatic axis may silently rescale and change the apparent difference.

Implementation

def percentage_point_change(previous_rate, current_rate):
    if not all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (previous_rate, current_rate)):
        raise ValueError("rates must be between zero and one")
    return (current_rate - previous_rate) * 100

change_points = percentage_point_change(0.74, 0.77)

Performance and operating cost

Scale formatting is O(M) for M plotted marks. The larger cost is review: test every filter state that changes axis bounds, zero visibility or label collisions. Cache formatted labels only when underlying rate and unit versions match.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not truncate a bar axis without making the baseline explicit.
  • Do not label a percentage-point movement as a relative percent.
  • Do not hide nonpositive observations when using a logarithmic scale.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Validation drill

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.

title: Paired-change charts: match entities before drawing a slope
summary: Use slope and dumbbell views only after the before-and-after population is reconciled.
body:
Use slope and dumbbell views only after the before-and-after population is reconciled.

The line encodes identity

A slope chart connects two measurements for the same entity. Its line claims a valid pair, not just two values with matching labels. If a store was renamed, split or absent in one period, resolve that identity before drawing. A join on display name can connect unrelated stores, while a broad outer join can make missing endpoints look like zero. Join cardinality should be checked at one row per entity and period. Record which entities were excluded from the paired population.

Choose difference or ratio deliberately

A dumbbell chart places two points on a shared quantitative scale; a slope chart emphasizes direction between endpoints. The axis unit and baseline decide whether a move appears large. A change from 47 to 81 is 34 units and about 72 percent of the starting value, but those answer different questions. For baseline zero, a percentage change is undefined. State which measure is encoded by the sorted order and put exact start, end and difference in accessible text. Axis rules apply to both forms.

Control clutter and crossings

With dozens of entities, labels and crossing segments become hard to follow. Sort by one declared endpoint or difference, keep label positions consistent, and consider small multiples or a ranked difference bar when comparison is more important than identity tracking. Highlight selected entities without fading the rest into illegibility. A connected pair should use a line style, endpoint labels or shape in addition to color. Accessible encodings matter when the positive and negative groups share a palette.

Check comparability across periods

Before-after values may use different denominator definitions, currencies, coverage windows or measurement instruments. Do not join a complete prior quarter to an incomplete current quarter. Record the cohort cutoff and period length. If the chart includes only entities observed in both periods, say how many were lost and whether they differ from those retained; survivorship can reverse the narrative. Provisional-period handling also applies when there are only two points.

Worked contract

def paired_depot_change(
    prior: dict[str, int | None], current: dict[str, int | None]
) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, int, int, int]], set[str]]:
    if any(value is not None and value < 0 for value in [*prior.values(), *current.values()]):
        raise ValueError("negative request count")
    matched = []
    excluded = set(prior) | set(current)
    for depot_id in sorted(set(prior) & set(current)):
        before, after = prior[depot_id], current[depot_id]
        if before is None or after is None:
            continue
        matched.append((depot_id, before, after, after - before))
        excluded.remove(depot_id)
    return matched, excluded

pairs, absent = paired_depot_change(
    {"depot-47": 47, "depot-81": 81, "depot-94": 31},
    {"depot-47": 81, "depot-81": None, "depot-109": 40})
assert pairs == [("depot-47", 47, 81, 34)]
assert absent == {"depot-81", "depot-94", "depot-109"}

Performance and operating cost

For P prior and C current entities, hash-set intersection and validation take O(P + C) expected time; sorting K matched IDs takes O(K log K), with O(P + C) temporary space. If an ordered warehouse query already supplies stable IDs, sorting can be handled upstream. The excluded set is part of the chart contract; deleting it to make the visualization tidy hides selection bias. A renderer still needs label-collision handling for crowded panels.

Common Mistakes

  • Connecting two stores with the same display name but different stable IDs.
  • Substituting zero for a missing endpoint.
  • Showing a percentage increase when the baseline is zero.
  • Ignoring entities absent from the second period when describing the population.

Validation drill

Compare 47 depots across two quarters. Plant a renamed depot, a split depot and four incomplete current-quarter records; reconcile identity and report matched and excluded counts before drawing slopes.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.
